::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain the idea of the bootstrap: **resampling the sample** to approximate a sampling distribution;
- implement the bootstrap in base R with `sample(x, replace = TRUE)` and `replicate()`;
- compute a **bootstrap standard error** and a **percentile confidence interval** for a mean, a median and a correlation;
- compare a bootstrap interval with the classical t-based interval;
- recognise situations in which the bootstrap is unreliable (very small samples, extremes, dependent data).
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(ggplot2)
library(rsample)
```

## 1. The problem: we have only one sample

In the [previous lesson](30-sampling-distributions.qmd) we learned that the uncertainty of an estimate is described by its **sampling distribution**, and we saw it by drawing thousands of samples from a population we had built ourselves.

In real research we cannot do that. We have **one** sample. For the mean we are lucky: theory gives the standard error $s/\sqrt n$ and the t-distribution gives a confidence interval. But what about

- the **median** of a skewed variable?
- a **correlation**?
- the ratio of two means, a trimmed mean, the 90th percentile, a model's prediction error…?

For many statistics there is no simple formula, or the formula relies on assumptions (normality, large $n$) that we are not willing to make. The **bootstrap**, proposed by Bradley Efron in 1979, offers a general, computer-based answer.

## 2. The idea: resample the sample

If we could sample repeatedly from the population, we would. We cannot, but we have the next best thing: the sample itself, which is our best picture of the population. The bootstrap **treats the sample as if it were the population** and draws new samples from it:

| | Real world (impossible) | Bootstrap world (possible) |
|---|---|---|
| "Population" | the true population | our sample of size $n$ |
| Samples | new samples of size $n$ from the population | **resamples** of size $n$ drawn *with replacement* from our sample |
| Statistic | $\hat\theta$ in each new sample | $\hat\theta^*$ in each resample |
| Variability | sampling distribution of $\hat\theta$ | bootstrap distribution of $\hat\theta^*$ |

The key assumption: **the variability of $\hat\theta^*$ around $\hat\theta$ mimics the variability of $\hat\theta$ around the true parameter $\theta$.**

Why *with replacement*? A resample of size $n$ drawn *without* replacement from $n$ values is just the same data shuffled. With replacement, some observations appear twice or three times and others not at all, exactly as a new random sample from the population would contain some kinds of units more often and others less.

## 3. The algorithm step by step

We use the ozone measurements in the built-in `airquality` data (New York, summer 1973). Ozone is right-skewed, so the mean and the median differ.

```{r}
#| label: ozone
ozone <- airquality$Ozone[!is.na(airquality$Ozone)]
n <- length(ozone)
c(n = n, mean = mean(ozone), median = median(ozone))
```

**Step 1 — draw one resample** of size $n$ with replacement and compute the statistic:

```{r}
#| label: one-resample
set.seed(1)
resample <- sample(ozone, size = n, replace = TRUE)
mean(resample)
```

Some days appear several times in the resample, others not at all:

```{r}
#| label: resample-counts
set.seed(1)
table(table(resample_id = sample(1:n, n, replace = TRUE)))
```

(The output reads: so many observations were drawn once, so many twice, and so on. On average only about 63% of the original observations appear in a resample; see the "Going deeper" box in Section 7.)

**Step 2 — repeat many times** (B = 5,000 is plenty here) and store each statistic:

```{r}
#| label: boot-mean
set.seed(1)
boot_means <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(ozone, replace = TRUE)))
```

`sample(x, replace = TRUE)` uses `size = length(x)` by default: exactly what the bootstrap needs.

**Step 3 — look at the bootstrap distribution:**

```{r}
#| label: fig-boot-mean
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the mean ozone level (5,000 resamples). The solid line is the sample mean; dashed lines delimit the middle 95% of bootstrap means."
ci_mean <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))

ggplot(data.frame(mean = boot_means), aes(mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#0072B2", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(ozone), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_mean, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap mean of ozone (ppb)", y = "Number of resamples")
```

**Step 4 — summarise the uncertainty.**

- The **bootstrap standard error** is the SD of the bootstrap statistics.
- The **percentile confidence interval** takes the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the bootstrap statistics.

```{r}
#| label: boot-mean-summary
sd(boot_means)              # bootstrap SE
sd(ozone) / sqrt(n)         # classical SE, for comparison
ci_mean                     # 95% percentile CI
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read these results

- The bootstrap SE, `r round(sd(boot_means), 2)`, is very close to the formula $s/\sqrt n =$ `r round(sd(ozone) / sqrt(n), 2)`. For the mean the bootstrap simply rediscovers what theory already knew — a reassuring check.
- The 95% percentile interval runs from `r round(ci_mean[1], 1)` to `r round(ci_mean[2], 1)` ppb: the range of mean ozone levels compatible with the data. [Confidence intervals](../08-inference/32-confidence-intervals.qmd) explains exactly what "95%" means.
- Your numbers will differ slightly with a different seed; increase `B` if the second decimal matters.
:::

### Comparison with the t-based interval

```{r}
#| label: t-vs-boot
t_ci <- t.test(ozone)$conf.int
rbind(t_based = t_ci[1:2], bootstrap = ci_mean)
```

The two intervals are similar. The bootstrap interval is slightly **asymmetric** around the mean, because the bootstrap distribution reflects the right skew of the data; the t interval is symmetric by construction. With $n =$ `r n` the CLT makes both reasonable for the mean.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the plug-in principle

Let $F$ be the unknown population distribution and $\hat F$ the **empirical distribution** of the sample, which puts probability $1/n$ on each observation. Sampling with replacement from the data *is* sampling from $\hat F$. The bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution of $\hat\theta = t(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$, $X_i \sim F$, by the distribution of $\hat\theta^* = t(X^*_1, \ldots, X^*_n)$, $X^*_i \sim \hat F$. Since $\hat F \to F$ as $n$ grows, the approximation improves with $n$.

The percentile interval is the simplest bootstrap CI. Refinements such as the **BCa** (bias-corrected and accelerated) interval correct for bias and skewness and are available in the `boot` package (`boot::boot.ci(type = "bca")`). Monte Carlo error from using a finite B is a separate, controllable issue: B ≈ 1,000 is usually enough for an SE, while a few thousand are advisable for percentile CIs.
:::

## 4. The real strength: statistics without a formula

### The median

The median is a natural summary for skewed data, but its standard error has no simple, assumption-free formula. For the bootstrap it makes no difference: replace `mean` with `median`.

```{r}
#| label: boot-median
set.seed(2)
boot_medians <- replicate(5000, median(sample(ozone, replace = TRUE)))
sd(boot_medians)
quantile(boot_medians, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boot-median
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the median ozone level. It is lumpy because the median of a resample can only be one of the observed values (or the midpoint of two)."
ggplot(data.frame(median = boot_medians), aes(median)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#009E73") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(ozone), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap median of ozone (ppb)", y = "Number of resamples")
```

The median of ozone is `r median(ozone)` ppb with a 95% bootstrap interval from `r round(quantile(boot_medians, 0.025), 1)` to `r round(quantile(boot_medians, 0.975), 1)` ppb. The SE of the median (`r round(sd(boot_medians), 2)`) is larger than the SE of the mean here; the median buys robustness at the price of some precision.

### A correlation

For a statistic computed from **pairs** of values, we must resample whole **rows** (units), keeping each pair together. We do this by resampling row *indices*. Example: the correlation between bill length and bill depth for Gentoo penguins.

```{r}
#| label: gentoo-cor
gentoo <- penguins[penguins$species == "Gentoo",
                   c("bill_len", "bill_dep")]
gentoo <- gentoo[complete.cases(gentoo), ]
r_obs <- cor(gentoo$bill_len, gentoo$bill_dep)
r_obs
```

```{r}
#| label: boot-cor
set.seed(3)
boot_cor <- replicate(5000, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(gentoo), replace = TRUE)   # resample rows
  cor(gentoo$bill_len[idx], gentoo$bill_dep[idx])
})
sd(boot_cor)
quantile(boot_cor, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boot-cor
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the correlation between bill length and bill depth in Gentoo penguins. Correlations cannot exceed 1, so the distribution is slightly skewed to the left."
ggplot(data.frame(r = boot_cor), aes(r)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#CC79A7", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r_obs, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(boot_cor, c(0.025, 0.975)),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap correlation", y = "Number of resamples")
```

The interval from `r round(quantile(boot_cor, 0.025), 2)` to `r round(quantile(boot_cor, 0.975), 2)` excludes 0 comfortably: longer Gentoo bills tend to be deeper. Compare with the classical interval of `cor.test()`, which relies on a normal approximation (the Fisher transformation):

```{r}
#| label: cor-test
cor.test(gentoo$bill_len, gentoo$bill_dep)$conf.int
```

### Summary of the three intervals

```{r}
#| label: ci-table
data.frame(
  statistic = c("mean ozone", "median ozone", "correlation (Gentoo)"),
  estimate  = c(mean(ozone), median(ozone), r_obs),
  boot_se   = c(sd(boot_means), sd(boot_medians), sd(boot_cor)),
  lower     = c(ci_mean[1], quantile(boot_medians, 0.025),
                quantile(boot_cor, 0.025)),
  upper     = c(ci_mean[2], quantile(boot_medians, 0.975),
                quantile(boot_cor, 0.975)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

Same three lines of code each time: resample, compute, summarise. This generality is why the bootstrap is used everywhere, from medians to machine-learning performance metrics.

## 5. When the bootstrap fails or is risky

The bootstrap is not magic: it can only reproduce variability that is visible **in the sample**.

### Very small samples

With 5 observations, a resample can only contain those 5 values, and the bootstrap distribution underestimates how different a new sample could be. Let us check how often a 95% interval actually contains the true mean (its **coverage**) when $n = 5$ and the data are normal:

```{r}
#| label: small-n-coverage
set.seed(4)
covers <- replicate(1000, {
  x <- rnorm(5)                                    # true mean is 0
  boot <- colMeans(matrix(sample(x, 5 * 1000, replace = TRUE), nrow = 5))
  pct <- quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
  tci <- t.test(x)$conf.int
  c(bootstrap = pct[[1]] < 0 & pct[[2]] > 0,
    t_based   = tci[1] < 0 & tci[2] > 0)
})
rowMeans(covers)
```

(`matrix(sample(...), nrow = 5)` draws 1,000 resamples at once as the columns of a matrix, and `colMeans()` gives their means — a fast alternative to `replicate()`.)

The "95%" percentile interval contains the true mean only about `r round(100 * rowMeans(covers)[["bootstrap"]])`% of the time: it is **too narrow**. The t interval, which builds the extra uncertainty of small samples into the t-distribution, keeps its promise (about `r round(100 * rowMeans(covers)[["t_based"]])`%). With small samples, prefer methods with good small-sample theory, or at least do not trust bootstrap intervals blindly.

### Extremes: the maximum

The bootstrap struggles with statistics that depend on one or two extreme observations. Consider the maximum of 30 values from $\text{Uniform}(0, 1)$; the true maximum of the population is 1.

```{r}
#| label: boot-max
set.seed(5)
x <- runif(30)
boot_max <- replicate(5000, max(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
max(x)
mean(boot_max == max(x))   # share of resamples whose max is the sample max
max(boot_max) > max(x)     # can a resample ever exceed the sample max?
```

About `r round(100 * mean(boot_max == max(x)))`% of the resamples have exactly the same maximum as the sample, and no resample can ever go beyond it. The bootstrap distribution is a spike, nothing like the true (continuous) sampling distribution of the maximum, and it gives no hint that the true value 1 lies above every observation.

### Dependent data

The basic bootstrap resamples observations **independently**, so it assumes the observations *are* independent. In a time series, today resembles yesterday; shuffling days destroys that structure and the bootstrap underestimates the uncertainty. A quick simulation with an autocorrelated series:

```{r}
#| label: boot-dependent
set.seed(6)
series <- as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.7), n = 100))
naive_se <- sd(replicate(2000, mean(sample(series, replace = TRUE))))

# the true SE, from many independent series generated the same way
true_se <- sd(replicate(2000, mean(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.7), n = 100))))
c(naive_bootstrap = naive_se, true = true_se)
```

`arima.sim()` generates a series in which each value depends on the previous one. The naive bootstrap SE is less than half the true SE: intervals would be far too optimistic. For time series, clustered or repeated-measures data, resample **blocks** of consecutive observations or whole **clusters** (e.g. all measurements of one patient) instead of single rows.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Resampling without replacement.** `sample(x)` only shuffles the data: every resample has the same mean and the "SE" is 0. Always `replace = TRUE`.
2. **Resampling columns separately.** For correlations, regressions or any multivariable statistic, resample **rows** (via indices), not each variable on its own — that destroys the relationship you are studying (Exercise 3).
3. **Thinking the bootstrap creates information.** It does not add data; it only re-uses the sample. If the sample is small or unrepresentative, so is the bootstrap.
4. **Bootstrapping dependent data as if it were independent** (time series, repeated measures, clusters). Resample the independent units.
5. **Too few resamples or no seed.** Use at least 1,000 resamples (more for percentile CIs) and `set.seed()` so results are reproducible.
:::

## 6. A tidy alternative: `rsample::bootstraps()`

The [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org) package **rsample**, which we will use for machine learning, provides the same resampling in a data-frame form. `bootstraps(data, times = B)` returns a table with one row per resample; each row holds a `split` object, and `analysis(split)` extracts the resampled data.

```{r}
#| label: rsample-boot
set.seed(3)
boots <- bootstraps(gentoo, times = 1000)
boots

boot_cor_tidy <- vapply(boots$splits, \(s) {
  d <- analysis(s)
  cor(d$bill_len, d$bill_dep)
}, numeric(1))

quantile(boot_cor_tidy, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

`vapply(..., numeric(1))` applies the function to every split and checks that each result is a single number (see [Iteration](../03-programming/17-iteration.qmd)). The interval agrees with our base-R version up to Monte Carlo noise. The advantage of `rsample` is not the bootstrap itself — three lines of base R suffice — but that the same objects plug directly into the modelling tools of [The ML workflow](../10-ml/44-ml-workflow.qmd).

## 7. Looking ahead: bootstrap aggregating ("bagging")

The bootstrap reappears in machine learning in a different role. A single decision tree is very sensitive to the exact data it is fitted on: change a few rows and the tree can change completely. **Bagging** (*bootstrap aggregating*) fits one tree to **each bootstrap resample** and **averages** their predictions. Averaging many noisy but different models reduces variance, just as averaging many observations reduces the SE of a mean. **Random forests** add one more trick (each split considers only a random subset of the variables) and are among the most widely used prediction methods; see [Random forests](../10-ml/46-random-forests.qmd).

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the 63.2% rule and out-of-bag observations

The probability that a given observation is **not** picked in any of the $n$ draws of a resample is $(1 - 1/n)^n \to e^{-1} \approx 0.368$. So each resample contains on average about 63.2% of the distinct original observations, and the remaining ≈ 36.8% are "out of bag". Random forests use these left-out observations as a free test set (the *out-of-bag error*). A one-line check:

```{r}
#| label: oob
set.seed(7)
mean(replicate(2000, mean(!(1:100 %in% sample(100, replace = TRUE)))))
```
:::

## 8. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Why must bootstrap resamples be drawn *with* replacement and have the same size as the original sample?

Without replacement, a resample of size $n$ is just a permutation of the data and every statistic stays the same. Same size $n$, because the variability of a statistic depends on the sample size: we want to mimic samples of the size we actually have.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. The bootstrap SE of the mean and $s/\sqrt n$ are almost identical. Why bother with the bootstrap then?

For the mean there is no need — but the bootstrap works in exactly the same way for statistics that have no simple SE formula (median, correlation, ratios, quantiles, model metrics). The agreement for the mean is a useful check that the method works.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. You have daily temperatures for one year and want an interval for the annual mean. Is the ordinary bootstrap appropriate?

No. Consecutive days are correlated, and resampling single days independently ignores that dependence, so the bootstrap SE would be too small. A block bootstrap (resampling runs of consecutive days) or a time-series model is needed.
:::

## 9. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — bootstrap a mean.** Bootstrap the mean fuel consumption `mpg` in `mtcars` with 5,000 resamples. Report the bootstrap SE and the 95% percentile interval, and compare with the t-based interval from `t.test()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_31_1
x <- mtcars$mpg
set.seed(1)
boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(x, replace = ______)))
sd(______)
quantile(boot, c(______, ______))
t.test(x)$conf.int
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_31_1"}
Resample with `replace = TRUE`; the SE is `sd(boot)`; the 95% percentile interval uses the quantiles 0.025 and 0.975.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_31_1"}
```r
x <- mtcars$mpg
set.seed(1)
boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
sd(boot)                          # about 1.04
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))   # about 18.1 to 22.2
t.test(x)$conf.int                # about 17.9 to 22.3
```
The bootstrap interval is a little narrower than the t interval: with only 32 cars the percentile bootstrap tends to be slightly optimistic (Section 5), while the t-distribution accounts for estimating the SD.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — bootstrap a median.** The built-in vector `rivers` contains the lengths (in miles) of 141 major North American rivers; it is strongly right-skewed. Compute the median and a 95% bootstrap percentile interval for it. Then draw a histogram of the bootstrap medians: why does it look lumpy?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_31_2
median(rivers)
set.seed(2)
boot_med <- replicate(5000, ______(sample(rivers, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_med, c(0.025, 0.975))
hist(boot_med, breaks = 40, main = "Bootstrap medians", xlab = "Miles")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_31_2"}
Replace the blank with the statistic you want to bootstrap: `median`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_31_2"}
```r
median(rivers)                                   # 425
set.seed(2)
boot_med <- replicate(5000, median(sample(rivers, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_med, c(0.025, 0.975))              # roughly 380 to 490
hist(boot_med, breaks = 40, main = "Bootstrap medians", xlab = "Miles")
```
With $n = 141$ (odd), the median of each resample is always one of the observed river lengths, so the bootstrap distribution can take only a limited set of values — hence the gaps and spikes. The interval is asymmetric around 425, reflecting the skew.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug the bootstrap.** A student wants a bootstrap interval for the correlation between `speed` and `dist` in the built-in `cars` data (observed $r \approx 0.81$) and writes the code below. The interval is centred near 0! Find and fix the bug.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_31_3
cor(cars$speed, cars$dist)
set.seed(3)
boot_r <- replicate(5000, {
  s <- sample(cars$speed, replace = TRUE)
  d <- sample(cars$dist, replace = TRUE)
  cor(s, d)
})
quantile(boot_r, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_31_3"}
The two variables are resampled independently, so a car's speed is paired with *another* car's stopping distance. Resample row indices with `idx <- sample(nrow(cars), replace = TRUE)` and use `cars$speed[idx]` and `cars$dist[idx]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_31_3"}
```r
set.seed(3)
boot_r <- replicate(5000, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(cars), replace = TRUE)
  cor(cars$speed[idx], cars$dist[idx])
})
quantile(boot_r, c(0.025, 0.975))   # about 0.70 to 0.88
```
Resampling the columns separately breaks the pairs and simulates a world with no relationship, so the "interval" was centred on 0. Resampling whole rows keeps each car's speed and distance together.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — predict the failure.** Draw a sample of 50 values from $\text{Uniform}(0, 10)$, so the true population maximum is 10. Before running the code, predict: (a) roughly what share of bootstrap maxima will equal the sample maximum? (b) Will the 95% percentile interval for the maximum contain 10?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_31_4
set.seed(4)
x <- runif(50, min = 0, max = 10)
max(x)
boot_max <- replicate(5000, max(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
mean(boot_max == ______)
quantile(boot_max, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_31_4"}
Compare each bootstrap maximum with `max(x)`. The chance that the largest observation is drawn at least once in 50 draws is $1 - (1 - 1/50)^{50}$.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_31_4"}
```r
mean(boot_max == max(x))              # about 0.64
1 - (1 - 1/50)^50                     # theory: 0.636
quantile(boot_max, c(0.025, 0.975))   # upper limit = max(x) < 10
```
About 64% of resamples contain the largest observation, so their maximum equals the sample maximum. No resample can exceed `max(x)`, so the interval never reaches the true value 10. For extremes, the bootstrap is the wrong tool.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — a difference between two groups.** For Adelie penguins, estimate the difference in mean body mass between males and females with a bootstrap CI. Resample **within each sex separately** (why?), and compare your interval with the Welch interval of `t.test(body_mass ~ sex, data = adelie)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
adelie <- penguins[penguins$species == "Adelie" & !is.na(penguins$sex) &
                     !is.na(penguins$body_mass), ]
m <- adelie$body_mass[adelie$sex == "male"]
f <- adelie$body_mass[adelie$sex == "female"]
mean(m) - mean(f)

set.seed(5)
boot_diff <- replicate(5000, {
  mean(sample(m, replace = TRUE)) - mean(sample(f, replace = TRUE))
})
quantile(boot_diff, c(0.025, 0.975))
t.test(body_mass ~ sex, data = adelie)$conf.int   # female - male: signs flip
```
The males are on average about 675 g heavier, and both intervals run from roughly 575 to 775 g (the `t.test()` interval is for female − male, so its signs are reversed). Resampling within each group keeps the group sizes fixed, as in the original design.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Step / function | Code | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| One resample | `sample(x, replace = TRUE)` | New sample of size $n$ from the data |
| Resample rows | `idx <- sample(nrow(df), replace = TRUE)`; `df[idx, ]` | Keep variables paired |
| Bootstrap distribution | `replicate(B, stat(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))` | Approximate sampling distribution |
| Bootstrap SE | `sd(boot)` | Precision of the estimate |
| Percentile CI | `quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))` | 95% interval |
| Tidy resampling | `rsample::bootstraps(df, times = B)`, `analysis(split)` | Same idea in data-frame form |

- The bootstrap **resamples the sample** with replacement to imitate drawing new samples from the population.
- The same three steps — resample, compute, summarise — give SEs and CIs for statistics **without a formula**.
- For the mean, bootstrap and t-based results agree closely when $n$ is moderate.
- It is unreliable for **very small samples**, **extremes** and **dependent data**; resample the independent units.
- Bootstrap + averaging = **bagging**, the core of random forests.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
